section.title: Hear a Just Cause
section.sectionRationale: An individual lament in the form of a legal plea, David appealing to God as righteous judge to examine his heart, vindicate his innocence against violent enemies, and keep him as the apple of God's eye. It closes with one of the Psalter's earliest hints of hope beyond death, awaking satisfied in God's presence.
section.thesis: David appeals boldly to God's own examination of his heart, asking to be kept as the apple of God's eye and hidden under His wings, and closes by anticipating a satisfaction found only in beholding God's face.
section.frameNote: Four movements: David's plea for a hearing of his righteous cause; his declaration of innocence tested by God Himself; his urgent request for protection as the apple of God's eye from violent enemies; and his closing hope of awaking satisfied in God's presence.

units.label: Hear my righteous plea
units.note: an appeal for a just hearing

verses.text: Hear, O LORD, my righteous plea; listen to my cry. Give ear to my prayer, it comes from lips free of deceit.
May my vindication come from Your presence; may Your eyes see what is right.

units.label: You have tested me and found no evil

verses.text: You have tried my heart; You have visited me in the night. You have tested me and found no evil; I have resolved not to sin with my mouth.

As for the deeds of men, by the word of Your lips 
I have avoided the ways of the violent.
My steps have held to Your paths; my feet have not slipped.

units.label: Keep me as the apple of Your eye

verses.text: I call on You, O God, for You will answer me. Incline Your ear to me; hear my words.

Show the wonders of Your {{chesed|loving devotion}}, You who save by Your right hand 
those who seek refuge from their foes.
Keep me as the {{ishon|apple of Your eye}}; hide me in the shadow of Your wings
from the wicked who assail me, from my mortal enemies who surround me.
They have closed their callous hearts; their mouths speak with arrogance.
They have tracked us down, and now surround us; their eyes are set to cast us to the ground,
like a lion greedy for prey, like a young lion lurking in ambush.
Arise, O LORD, confront them! Bring them to their knees; deliver me from the wicked by Your sword,

from such men, O LORD, by Your hand, from men of the world whose portion is in this life. May You fill the bellies of Your treasured ones and satisfy their sons, so they leave their abundance to their children.
As for me, I will behold Your face in righteousness; when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion. David asks God to show the wonders of this loving devotion specifically to those who take refuge in Him, grounding his plea not in his own merit but in God's covenant character.

ishon.gloss: Literally 'little man,' the pupil of the eye, the small reflection one sees of oneself in another's eye, used idiomatically for something treasured and carefully guarded. David asks to be kept as precious and protected as the pupil of God's own eye.

basic.context: David appeals to God as judge, asking Him to hear a righteous cause spoken without deceit. He declares that God Himself has already tested his heart at night and found no evil in him regarding the specific charges his enemies bring. He then urgently asks to be kept as the apple of God's eye and hidden under His wings from violent enemies who stalk him like lions, appealing for God to arise and deliver him. The psalm closes with a quiet but striking hope: David expects to awake and be satisfied, beholding God's face in righteousness.
basic.hermeneutics: This is not a claim to sinless perfection but a legal plea of innocence regarding specific false accusations and violent pursuit; David appeals to God's own searching examination as his defense. Its closing verse offers an early, undeveloped hint of hope beyond death that later revelation, especially the resurrection of Christ, brings into full light.
basic.originalLanguages: David asks God to show the wonders of His chesed, covenant loving devotion, to those who seek refuge in Him, and pleads to be kept as ishon, the apple or pupil of God's eye, a vivid image of being treasured and closely guarded, hidden further still in the shadow of God's wings.
basic.typology: David's plea to be vindicated by God's own examination and kept as the apple of His eye anticipates the perfect innocence of Christ, who alone could truly say His accusers found no fault in Him, and who was vindicated by God through the resurrection.
basic.christ: David's confidence of a righteous vindication before God and his hope of beholding God's face anticipate the greater righteousness of Christ, the only truly innocent sufferer, whose resurrection and ascension are the ultimate vindication this psalm reaches toward, and through whom believers now have the hope of one day beholding God's face, Revelation 22:4.
basic.god: God is shown as a righteous judge who tests hearts honestly, as a refuge whose loving devotion protects those who flee to Him, and as the one whose presence alone finally satisfies, a satisfaction awaiting even beyond death.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 32:10 uses the same image of the apple of the eye for God's care of Israel. 1 Peter 2:22-23 shows Christ as the truly innocent sufferer who entrusted Himself to the righteous judge. Revelation 22:4 promises believers will see God's face.
basic.oneStory: David's plea to be examined, vindicated, and kept as precious as the apple of God's eye reaches toward a satisfaction found only in beholding God's face, a hope the whole Bible shows is secured for all who trust in Christ, the truly innocent one whom God has vindicated and exalted.

context.literary:
Psalm 17 is a courtroom prayer, and the legal vocabulary sets its shape. It opens with a petition to be heard, verses 1 to 2, moves to evidence given under oath, verses 3 to 5, turns to the appeal for protection, verses 6 to 9, describes the accusers, verses 10 to 12, and ends with a verdict sought and a hope stated, verses 13 to 15. The heading in the Hebrew Psalter calls it simply a prayer of David, and it is one of several psalms in this part of the Psalter where David is hunted and asks God to judge.

Notice the movement of the body. The psalm begins with the ear, 'Hear', 'listen', 'Give ear', verses 1 and 6, and ends with the face and the eye: God's eyes are asked to 'see what is right' in verse 2, David asks to be the pupil of God's eye in verse 8, and he expects at the close to behold God's face in verse 15. Prayer that begins by asking to be heard ends in sight.

The enemies are described in a run of bodily images as well: closed hearts, arrogant mouths, eyes set to cast David down, and finally the lion, verses 10 to 12. Then David sets against that picture his own body, lips free of deceit in verse 1, a mouth resolved against sin in verse 3, feet that have not slipped in verse 5. Verse 14 is the hinge between the wicked and the righteous, and it is famously hard to translate, as the BSB footnote admits. The final verse begins with a strongly marked 'As for me', answering the 'As for the deeds of men' of verse 4 and the 'men of the world' of verse 14.
context.historical:
The psalm is headed as David's, and its setting is a man surrounded by hostile people who stalk him like a predator. First Samuel gives two obvious backdrops. In the years of Saul's pursuit David twice had Saul in his power and refused to strike, and he told Saul, 'there is no evil or rebellion in my hands,' 1 Samuel 24:11. That is the same kind of claim David makes here, a claim about a particular charge and not about his whole character. The other likely setting is the flight from Absalom, when David's own household turned on him. The psalm does not say which, and its language of a lion in ambush, verse 12, fits either.

The language of the courtroom matters for the first hearers. In Israel a person accused, with no earthly court able to help, could bring the case before the LORD at the sanctuary. The prayer for 'vindication' from God's presence, verse 2, has that setting in mind, as do the references to God testing the heart, verse 3, and the appeal that God's eyes 'see what is right'. The night visit of verse 3 may describe a time of prayer or of trouble, and the text does not say which.

The images of protection would also have been familiar. The 'shadow of Your wings' called to mind the outstretched wings of the cherubim above the ark, and Ruth is told she has taken refuge 'under whose wings,' Ruth 2:12. The lion that lies in ambush was a real danger to shepherds, and David knew that danger firsthand.
context.canonical:
The apple of the eye reaches back to Deuteronomy 32:10-11, where the LORD found Israel in a howling desert and 'guarded him as the apple of His eye,' and then spread His wings like an eagle over its young. Psalm 17:8 fuses those two pictures, eye and wings, and asks that what God did for the nation be done for one hunted man. Zechariah 2:8 later returns to the phrase: whoever touches God's people 'touches the apple of His eye.' The wings appear again in Psalm 36:7, Psalm 91:4 and Ruth 2:12, and Jesus takes up the same image of a hen with her chicks when He weeps over Jerusalem, Matthew 23:37.

The wicked whose 'portion is in this life,' verse 14, are set against Psalm 16:5 and Psalm 73:26, where God Himself is the portion of His people. The last verse belongs with a group of Psalms that reach beyond the grave: Psalm 16:9-11, Psalm 49:15 and Psalm 73:24-26. Job says, 'in my flesh I will see God,' Job 19:26, and Daniel 12:2 speaks of those who 'sleep in the dust' and 'awake.' In the New Testament Peter uses Psalm 16 at Pentecost, Acts 2:25-28, and the promise to see God becomes central: 'they will see God,' Matthew 5:8; 'we will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2; 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4.

Finally, Jesus' own trials match the psalm's courtroom, as Pilate says he finds no basis for a charge, John 19:4, and a centurion at the cross calls Him righteous, Luke 23:47.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted his fellow Israelites, and later every worshiper, to learn how to pray when they are in the right and the other side is stronger. The psalm gives permission to say plainly, before God, that a charge is false. It does not ask God to overlook the facts; it asks Him to look at them. Verse 3 is the centre of the argument: God has already examined the heart, by night, and the sentence is that David is clean of the crime named.

The psalm also protects that boldness from arrogance. David never asks for a reward on the strength of his record; his appeal for protection in verses 7 and 8 rests on God's covenant loyalty, 'Show the wonders of Your loving devotion,' and not on his own steps. The innocence is the reason he can speak, but the mercy is the reason he can hope.

Finally, verses 14 and 15 tell the worshiper what to want. The wicked are content with a full stomach and something to leave the children. David is not against those good things and even asks that God's people have them, but he sets them beneath the vision of God, which alone satisfies. A first hearer, hunted and hungry, is taught to treat God's face as the greater prize.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's claim to innocence in a specific case, and it does not prescribe that every believer stand on their own record. Read as a template, verses 3 to 5 could tempt anyone to boast, and Paul warns that no one is justified before God by works, Romans 3:20. The safer reading is that David appeals to God's searching knowledge in a matter where he really was wronged, exactly as we may say 'I did not do this' when falsely accused, while adding the request of Psalm 139:23-24 to be searched further.

The prayer for God to 'bring them to their knees,' verse 13, is likewise a cry to the judge and not a licence to take vengeance. David leaves the sword with God. What carries forward is the pattern: bring the injustice to God, say honestly what you know, ask for shelter, and set your hope on seeing Him.

debates.question: Does verse 15's hope of 'awaking satisfied' refer to a full doctrine of bodily resurrection or something more limited?

views.label: It expresses a genuine, if not fully developed, hope of resurrection and future vision of God, an early seed that later revelation brings to full clarity
views.case: The language of awaking and beholding God's face closely parallels later resurrection hope in Daniel 12:2 and is read by much of the Christian tradition as anticipating bodily resurrection, though David himself likely had limited clarity about how this would occur.

views.label: It primarily expresses hope of waking each morning to renewed fellowship with God after a night of trial, a this life confidence rather than an explicit resurrection claim
views.case: The immediate context concerns deliverance from present enemies rather than death itself, and 'awake' may simply picture the morning after a night of prayer and testing, as in verse 3's reference to God visiting him in the night. Psalm 3:5 uses waking in exactly that sense, 'I wake again, for the LORD sustains me.'

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm the verse expresses genuine confidence in God's presence as ultimately satisfying; Christian reading, informed by the fuller resurrection hope revealed in Christ, rightly hears in this verse an early note of the hope fully realized in the gospel.

debates.question: What does David mean by saying God 'found no evil' in him, verse 3, when other psalms confess sin?

views.label: A claim of innocence on the specific charge
views.case: The context is a false accusation, verses 1 to 4, and David's statement about his mouth and his steps answers what his enemies allege. First Samuel 24:11 records a real occasion on which he could say something similar. On this view David is not denying he is a sinner, only that the accusation is untrue.

views.label: A claim about the basic direction of his life
views.case: Others hear a wider claim of covenant faithfulness, that David is among those who 'seek refuge' in God, verse 7, and whose way has not been the way of the violent, verse 4. Such a claim is compatible with confession, since Psalm 32 and Psalm 51 are also David's.

views.label: A voice that finds its full owner in Christ
views.case: Because the language reaches so far, 'You have tested me and found no evil,' many Christian readers hear the words as fitting only the Messiah, who could say, 'He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22. David is then the type, and the words are true of him in part and of Christ completely.

debates.bearing: Every reading keeps the psalm from becoming a boast of sinless perfection. What matters for prayer is that the heart is opened to God's examination, as in Psalm 139:23-24, and that the one who prays trusts God's mercy as well as his own innocence.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 piles up three verbs of examination, and each has its own picture. 'You have tried my heart' uses bachan, to test, the assayer's word for weighing metal; 'You have visited me' uses paqad, the verb for God's coming to look in on someone, whether for care or for reckoning; and 'You have tested me' uses tsaraf, to refine in the fire, as in Psalm 66:10, 'You have refined us like silver.' The refiner's word returns in Psalm 18:30, where the word of the LORD is 'flawless,' from the same root. David is not merely inspected but smelted, and he says nothing was found. The last phrase of verse 3, about his mouth, is difficult in Hebrew and translators divide over where it belongs, which is why the BSB reads it as a resolve.

In verse 8 the ishon, 'apple of Your eye,' is literally 'little man,' a diminutive of the ordinary word for man, and the BSB footnote gives the fuller picture, 'the pupil, the daughter of' the eye. The pupil is the tiny figure you see reflected when you look into someone's eye. To be that is to be looked at, up close, by God. The word is used of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:10 and of a father's teaching in Proverbs 7:2, where the son is told to guard it as the apple of his eye. The psalm asks that God guard David as carefully as a person guards his own sight.

In verse 13 the verb rendered 'confront' is qadam, to go before or to meet, and 'bring them to their knees' comes from kara, to bow or kneel. The same verb gives 'They collapse' in Psalm 20:8. Their fall is pictured as a kneeling down, not a slaying.

Verse 14 turns on the word cheleq, 'portion.' The enemies' portion, the share they have been dealt, is chayyim, this life. The same noun is used of God as the believer's own share in Psalm 16:5 and Psalm 73:26. One group has a portion in this life, the other has God.

In verse 15 'when I awake' is a form of the verb qits, to awake, and the object of the 'satisfied' is temunah, which the older English versions render 'likeness.' Temunah is the word used of the 'form of the LORD' that Moses beheld, Numbers 12:8, and of the form Israel did not see at Sinai, Deuteronomy 4:12. So the last line says: I shall be satisfied to wake in Your likeness, or Your form. It is not a philosophical hope but a hope of beholding.

typology.fulfillment: The lion lurking to bring David down is a picture of the enemy's intent, and the New Testament takes the same picture up of the devil, who 'prowls around like a roaring lion, looking for someone to devour,' 1 Peter 5:8. David's rescue from the lion's mouth anticipates the Son of David, who was surrounded by enemies at the cross, yet whose death 'destroyed him who holds the power of death,' Hebrews 2:14. The type falls short because David's deliverance was from a human enemy for a season; Christ's is the final defeat of the enemy behind all enemies.

typology.type: The plea for a public verdict, verses 1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: David asks that his vindication come 'from Your presence.' The greater Son of David was tried before Pilate, who said he found no basis for a charge, John 19:4, and before Herod and the priests, and was condemned regardless. His vindication came from God's presence in the resurrection, when He was 'vindicated by the Spirit,' 1 Timothy 3:16, and seated at God's right hand, Ephesians 1:20. The type falls short because David's verdict concerned one charge; Christ's vindication declares His whole life right and, by union with Him, ours.

typology.type: Kept as the apple of God's eye under the shadow of His wings, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: Israel was 'the apple of His eye' in the wilderness, Deuteronomy 32:10, and David asks for the same care. Jesus says He longed to gather Jerusalem 'as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings,' Matthew 23:37, taking to Himself the divine role of the sheltering wing. The correspondence deepens at the cross, where the one sheltering became the one exposed so that His people could be safe, Isaiah 53:5. The type falls short because David's shelter was from enemy swords; Christ's shelter is from the wrath of God itself.

typology.type: Waking to behold the face of God, verse 15
typology.fulfillment: David's closing hope points to a day of awakening and sight. Christ is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and His resurrection is the pledge that David's confidence was well placed. What David hoped, believers will see: 'we shall see face to face,' 1 Corinthians 13:12; 'we will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2. The type falls short because David's language is a hope; in Christ it is a promise with an empty tomb behind it.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by its likeness to His trial. David asks a just hearing and a public verdict, and no one in the Gospels received a less just hearing than Jesus. Pilate says, 'I find no basis for a charge against Him,' John 19:4, and washes his hands, Matthew 27:24. Even the centurion at the cross concludes, 'Surely this was a righteous man,' Luke 23:47. David could claim tested innocence about certain charges; only Jesus could stand under the refiner's fire and be found without sin, 'tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. Peter draws the same line when he quotes Isaiah about Jesus, 'He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, and says He 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. That last phrase is Psalm 17 in a sentence: the innocent sufferer appealing over the heads of his accusers to the true Judge.

It leads to Christ by the promise of vindication. David asks that the verdict come 'from Your presence.' In Jesus that verdict was given by resurrection. Paul says Christ was 'raised to life' as the one who intercedes for us, Romans 8:34, and that God raised Him and 'seated Him at His right hand,' Ephesians 1:20. The right hand of God in Psalm 17:7 is the hand that saves those who take refuge, and Christ sits at that hand.

It leads to Christ by contrast with the wicked of verse 14. Their portion is in this life; Christ became poor and gave up His life, and His portion is now the Father's presence. He also gave His people the same portion, so that Paul can say the Lord's people are 'heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ,' Romans 8:17.

The close of the psalm belongs to Him as well. Christ is the one who rises and beholds the Father's face, and through Him 'we will see Him as He is,' 1 John 3:2. It is a hope believers can hold only because the one who was innocent bore the guilty in His body, 1 Peter 3:18.

A word of caution is in order. Psalm 17 is not a Messianic psalm in the way Psalm 22 is, and the New Testament does not quote it. The connection is by pattern, the righteous sufferer who trusts God, and by the fulfilment of the hope of verse 15 in the resurrection, and readers should not make David's every phrase a prophecy.
study.god:
The psalm shows God as one who examines, and as one who is near. He tries the heart, he visits by night, and nothing in David's account is hidden from Him. That is what makes the prayer bold and safe at the same time: a plea that can only be made to someone who already knows the truth. The doctrine of God's knowledge is not a threat here but a comfort, since the God who sees all sees also that this man is wronged.

He is a judge who is not swayed by the size of the enemy. David's accusers are many and violent and have the upper hand, yet the psalm treats them as people who will kneel, verse 13. God's justice is his sword, and David asks that it be drawn against wickedness, not against his own person. The God of the psalm is not neutral between the wicked and the righteous.

He is tender. The two images of verse 8 are among the most intimate pictures of divine care in the Psalter. The apple of the eye is the most guarded part of the body, and the wings picture God as a protective bird over her young, as Deuteronomy 32:11 pictured the eagle over the nest. The God who can be asked to arise with a sword, verse 13, is the same God who can be asked to hide His child in His shadow. Power and gentleness are held together in one person.

He is the God of covenant loyalty. David does not say 'reward my innocence' but 'Show the wonders of Your loving devotion,' verse 7. The wonder is that God saves, by His right hand, those who run to Him for refuge. Refuge is the psalm's central movement, and it is grounded in what God is, not in what David has done.

He is also the God who satisfies. Verse 14 grants that God gives daily bread and family blessings to His people, and even to the wicked in this life, but verse 15 says the deepest satisfaction is God Himself. That teaches the worshiper what God is for. He is not first a means to safety or comfort but the goal of the person who prays. A right doctrine of God ends in seeing Him.

For worship, this means we can pray for justice honestly, with our hands open, and then let the prayer end where David's does, in quiet confidence, waiting to wake in God's presence.

crossReferences.note: The source of the apple-of-the-eye image. The LORD found Israel in a howling wilderness, guarded them like the pupil of His eye and spread His wings over them like an eagle. David borrows both pictures in Psalm 17:8 and asks for one man what God once did for a nation.

One of the scenes that may lie behind the psalm. David holds a piece of Saul's robe and says he has no evil or rebellion in his hands, then leaves judgment to the LORD. It shows what David's claim to innocence means: refusing to take vengeance and trusting God to judge.

The other side of Psalm 17:3. Where David says God has tested him and found nothing, here he asks God to search further, 'See if there is any offensive way in me.' The two prayers belong together: confidence about the accusation and humility about the heart.

The LORD is 'my chosen portion,' set against the men of verse 14 whose portion is in this life. The word portion joins the two psalms, and Psalm 16 goes on to its own hope beyond death, verses 9 to 11, just as Psalm 17 closes with waking and sight.

The poet nearly stumbles over the prosperity of the wicked, then sees that God is 'my portion forever.' It works out the contrast of Psalm 17:14 to 15 at more length, the full stomach of the wicked against the presence of God, and it also reaches beyond death.

God says He speaks with Moses 'face to face' and that he 'sees the form of the LORD.' The Hebrew word for form is the one behind the 'likeness' of Psalm 17:15. David hopes for what Moses was given in a measure, a real seeing of God.

Many who 'sleep in the dust of the earth will awake.' The picture of waking from death makes it likely that the word awake in Psalm 17:15 carried echoes of resurrection for later readers, even if David's own understanding was partial.

'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.' Jesus takes the theme of David's tested heart and clean lips and promises the very vision with which the psalm ends. Seeing God is the reward of a heart that has been made clean.

Peter presents Jesus as the pattern of the righteous sufferer, no sin, no deceit, no retaliation, entrusting Himself to the Judge who judges justly. It is the pattern of Psalm 17 lived out perfectly, and the ground on which sinners may take refuge.

Jesus longs to gather Jerusalem under His wings like a hen with her chicks, but they were unwilling. He takes for Himself the protective wings of Psalm 17:8, and shows that the shelter is offered and can be refused.
'We will see Him as He is.' John gives the New Testament answer to Psalm 17:15. Believers are already children, and the seeing is still ahead, promised for the day of Christ's appearing.
'They will see His face.' The last chapter of the Bible fulfils the last line of the psalm, in the city where God's presence is not veiled and His servants no longer need to wait to be satisfied.

study.oneStory:
The story of the whole Bible begins with people who walked with God and were unashamed in His sight, and it moves to a world of violence and false accusation where a righteous man has to plead for a hearing. Psalm 17 lives in that broken middle, and its question is the one Genesis 3 left open: after the fall, how can a person stand before God and how can anyone find safety? The psalm gives two answers. The first is that God looks, and judges rightly. The second is that God hides His people in His own shadow.

Behind the psalm are the stories of Israel's wilderness, where God found His people in a desert and guarded them, Deuteronomy 32:10, and Israel's kings, who were meant to trust the LORD more than their horses and swords. David is the king under attack, and his prayer shows what the true king does when he is outnumbered: he goes to God's courtroom and God's wings.

The psalm also looks ahead. Verse 15 is one of the early notes in the Old Testament of a hope beyond death, and it joins Job 19:26, Psalm 16 and Daniel 12:2. The prophets will sharpen it, and Jesus will make it certain. The righteous sufferer of verses 1 to 5 finds His fullest form in Christ, tried by the refiner's fire and without sin, Hebrews 4:15, condemned and yet vindicated by God, raised and seated at the right hand.

The Bible ends where Psalm 17 hopes to end. In the new creation 'They will see His face,' Revelation 22:4, and the sight that David craved is no longer a distant hope. The psalm's opening request, that God's eyes 'see what is right,' is answered when every wrong has been put right and every believer, hidden through the long night, wakes and is satisfied, Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: What kind of prayer is Psalm 17, in its overall form?

options.text: A legal plea of innocence, appealing to God as righteous judge against violent, false accusers.
options.note: The psalm's language of vindication, testing, and a righteous hearing marks it as a legal appeal.

options.text: A hymn of pure celebration with no element of complaint.
options.note: The psalm contains urgent complaint and plea against enemies, not pure celebration.

options.text: A wisdom psalm offering general life advice.
options.note: While it has some reflective elements, its dominant form is a legal lament and plea, not general wisdom instruction.

options.text: A psalm of corporate national lament over exile.
options.note: The psalm is personal and individual in its complaint, not focused on national exile.

quiz.q: What does David claim in verses 3-5 regarding God's testing of him?

options.text: That God Himself tested his heart at night and found no evil regarding the specific accusations against him.
options.note: David appeals to God's own examination as evidence of his innocence in this specific matter.

options.text: That he has never sinned in any way throughout his entire life.
options.note: This overstates the claim; David pleads specific innocence regarding these accusations, not sinless perfection generally.

options.text: That his enemies have also confirmed his innocence.
options.note: It is God's testing, not the enemies' confirmation, that David appeals to as evidence.

options.text: That he no longer needs to pray for God's guidance.
options.note: David continues to appeal urgently to God throughout the psalm, showing ongoing dependence on prayer.

quiz.q: What does David ask for in verse 8, and what does the image mean?

options.text: To be kept as the apple of God's eye, ishon, a picture of being treasured and carefully guarded.
options.note: This vivid idiom pictures something as precious and closely watched as the pupil of one's own eye.

options.text: To receive literal physical healing for an eye ailment.
options.note: The phrase is a figurative idiom for being treasured, not a literal medical request.

options.text: To gain greater physical eyesight for battle.
options.note: The request is about being protected and treasured by God, not about physical vision.

options.text: To be given prophetic visions of the future.
options.note: This misunderstands the idiom, which concerns being precious and protected, not receiving visions.

quiz.q: What hope does David express in the psalm's closing verse, verse 15?

options.text: That he will behold God's face in righteousness and awake satisfied in His presence.
options.note: This closing hope reaches beyond David's immediate circumstances toward lasting satisfaction in God's presence.

options.text: That his enemies will convert and become his friends.
options.note: The psalm's closing hope concerns David's own vindication and satisfaction in God, not his enemies' conversion.

options.text: That he will receive great material wealth in this life.
options.note: Verse 14 contrasts David's hope with 'men of the world whose portion is in this life,' distinguishing his hope from material gain.

options.text: That his descendants alone will benefit from God's blessing.
options.note: While verse 14 mentions descendants of the wicked, David's own personal hope in verse 15 is about beholding God's face himself.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's closing hope connect to the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates the fuller hope of resurrection and beholding God's face secured for believers through Christ, as in Revelation 22:4.
options.note: David's early, undeveloped hint of hope beyond death finds its full clarity and fulfillment in the resurrection secured by Christ.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to any New Testament teaching.
options.note: Its language of awaking and beholding God's face closely parallels New Testament resurrection and beatific vision themes.

options.text: It predicts the specific date of Christ's second coming.
options.note: The psalm expresses a hope of presence with God, not a specific predicted date for any future event.

options.text: It refers only to David's hope for a peaceful night's sleep with no further significance.
options.note: This understates the verse's deeper hope, widely read as anticipating a satisfaction beyond ordinary rest.

questions: David appeals to God's own examination of his heart rather than defending himself in his own words. Where do you need to bring an accusation or misunderstanding honestly to God rather than only trying to defend yourself?

David asks to be kept as the apple of God's eye and hidden under His wings. What would it look like this week to actually rest in that kind of treasured protection rather than trying to protect yourself?

David distinguishes his hope from 'men of the world whose portion is in this life' who look only for present abundance. Where might you be tempted to measure your life's success only by what you can gain or enjoy now?

David's closing hope is simply to behold God's face and be satisfied. What competing sources of satisfaction, achievement, comfort, approval, are you tempted to settle for instead of that deeper satisfaction found only in God's presence?

Christ, the truly innocent sufferer, entrusted Himself to the Father rather than defending Himself before His accusers. How does His example shape the way you respond when you are wrongly accused or mistreated?

translationNotes.note: Apple of Your eye renders ishon, literally 'little man,' referring to the pupil, where a small reflection of oneself can be seen, an idiom for something treasured and carefully guarded.
When I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence is one of the Psalter's earliest hints of hope beyond death, later developed fully in New Testament resurrection teaching.
